title: How a Church Should Make Decisions
subtitle: A practical guide to church decision making, governance, and congregational dynamics, covering process, spiritual authority, and how to decide without dividing the body.

sections.title: Before You Ask How, Ask Who
sections.body:
Most church conflicts about decisions are not really about the decision. They are about who had the right to make it, and the church never settled that question before the fight began. A congregation that has never clarified who decides what will relitigate authority every time something hard comes up, and it will exhaust itself doing it.

The New Testament shows real leaders with real authority, elders who lead and the congregation who follows, but it also shows a congregation that is not a passive crowd. When a man had to be removed in Corinth, Paul addressed the whole church. When leaders were chosen in Acts, the whole body was involved in setting them apart. Authority in the church is neither a dictatorship nor a democracy. It is leaders who genuinely lead and a people who genuinely affirm, each with a role the other cannot take.

Not every decision belongs to everyone. The color of the carpet does not need a congregational vote, and the doctrine of the church does not need a staff memo. Wisdom is knowing which decision sits at which level, the daily ones with the staff, the directional ones with the elders, the truly weighty ones, the pastor, the budget, the building, the constitution, before the whole congregation. Sort that out in calm seasons, write it down, and you will have spared yourself a hundred fights about process when you needed to be talking about substance.

sections.title: Good Decisions Have a Shape
sections.body:
A church that decides by impulse will decide badly, and a church that decides by exhaustion, whoever is still arguing at ten at night, will decide worse. Good decisions have a shape, an order they move through, and skipping a step is how you end up reversing yourself in six months.

It begins with the actual question, defined clearly, because half of all bad decisions are answers to a question no one took the time to state. Then information, real information, gathered honestly, including the cost and the case against. Then prayer that is not a bookend but the center, because the church is asking God what to do and ought to mean it. Then counsel, widening the circle to the people the decision will affect, because the wisdom to make it well is rarely held by the few who happen to hold the authority. Only then the decision, and then clear communication of it, and then the patience to let it prove itself.

The rushed church skips to the decision and backfills the rest. The paralyzed church gets stuck in information and never decides at all. Between them is a process that honors both the seriousness of the matter and the people it will touch. A decision that has moved through prayer, counsel, and honest information will stand, because the church can see that it was not the whim of a few but the discernment of the body.

sections.title: What Actually Happens in the Room
sections.body:
Every church has a real decision-making process and an official one, and they are not always the same. The official one is in the bylaws. The real one runs through the family that has been there four generations, the donor everyone is afraid of, the matriarch whose blessing a thing needs to survive. A leader who knows only the official process will be blindsided by the real one again and again.

This is not corruption. It is human community, and pretending it does not exist is naive. The wise leader does the relational work before the formal vote, talking with the people whose influence is real, hearing their concerns, addressing them honestly, long before the matter reaches the floor. Not to manipulate, but to lead, because a leader who springs a major decision on a congregation cold has not respected them, and they will punish the disrespect by killing the proposal.

There is a line here and it matters. Honoring the real dynamics of a congregation is wisdom. Becoming captive to them, letting the loudest voice or the largest checkbook decide what God has called the church to do, is cowardice with a strategy attached. Listen to everyone. Fear no one. The leader who has prepared the ground honestly and still leads where God has called, even past the powerful person who says no, is doing the actual work of leadership. The one who only ever does what the influential will allow is not leading. He is counting votes.

sections.title: Decide for Unity, Not Just for Outcome
sections.body:
A church can win the decision and lose the church. You can get the vote, pass the motion, carry the day, and walk out of the meeting with a congregation quietly bleeding from a wound that will open in a year. The outcome was never the only thing at stake. The body was.

This is why a narrow majority on a major decision should frighten a leader rather than satisfy him. A fifty-two percent vote to take on a building debt is not a mandate. It is a split waiting to surface, forty-eight percent of the church who now feel run over, and they will not forget it. The Jerusalem council in Acts labored toward a conclusion that seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to the whole assembly, a unity, not a squeaker. On the weighty matters, the goal is not to win but to bring the body to a place where it can move together, even if that means waiting longer than the leaders would like.

This does not mean the loudest objector gets a veto over everything. Some people will oppose anything, and a church held hostage to its most negative member will never move. But there is a difference between leading past a chronic complainer and bulldozing a genuinely divided congregation, and a leader who cannot tell the difference will leave a trail of split churches behind him. Decide in a way that keeps the body together. A right decision rammed through a wounded church may not have been worth what it cost.

sections.title: It Seemed Good to the Holy Spirit
sections.body:
There is a phrase in the book of Acts that ought to terrify us and comfort us at once. It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us. The early church believed, actually believed, that when the body sought God together and reached a conclusion, the Spirit of God was in the room and in the outcome. We say we believe that. Our decision-making usually reveals that we do not.

We decide like a business with a prayer at the start, run the numbers, count the votes, manage the politics, and treat the prayer as a formality we have already discounted. But if the church is the body of Christ, and if the Spirit indwells it, then decision-making is a spiritual act before it is a procedural one, and the question underneath every other question is not what do we want but what is God doing here, and are we willing to do it.

I have led churches through decisions where I forgot that, where I wanted my outcome more than I wanted God's will, and I dressed my preference in the language of discernment. The church can usually tell. A congregation that decides on its knees, that genuinely seeks the mind of Christ and submits to it, becomes something the consultants cannot manufacture. It becomes a people who can say, about the hard thing they chose, that it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us. May the things we decide be the kind of things he would put his name to.
